title: A Thought Experiment on Retrieval Practice
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins uses a thought experiment - four students (A, B, C, D) completing the same five-question retrieval quiz in different ways - to interrogate common classroom assumptions about what 'good' retrieval practice looks like. Drawing on the principles that 'memory is the residue of thought' and 'whoever does the thinking, does the learning,' he argues that Student D, who writes only the simplest complete answers to all five questions quickly, likely learns the most, because writing provides accountability that the student actually retrieved the answer, without wasting time on elaborate sentence construction that Adam Boxer calls 'busy tricking.' He contrasts this with Student A (writes full sentences, only completes 4/5 in the time available), Student B (focuses so hard on neat handwriting that the content is barely thought about), and Student C (thinks without writing, theoretically 5/5 but unverifiable and relying entirely on trust). Robbins's central critique is that many schools implicitly encourage the A/B approach because it 'looks nicer' in student books for quality-assurance purposes, even though this undermines the cognitive purpose retrieval practice is meant to serve. He extends the argument briefly to feedback, favouring cold-calling and tracked responses over simple self-reported hands-up confidence checks.
points: Robbins's thought experiment concludes that Student D - who writes the simplest complete answers to all five questions - is the strongest retrieval-practice performer, because writing provides accountability without wasting time on the elaborate sentence construction that Adam Boxer calls 'busy tricking.'

His critique of common school practice: many schools implicitly encourage full-sentence retrieval answers 'so students can look back in their books if they are stuck,' which Robbins argues misunderstands the point of retrieval practice.

Student C's case (thinking without writing) illustrates a core epistemic problem with retrieval practice: theoretically it can produce full recall, but without written evidence 'we are relying a lot on trust' that the thinking genuinely happened.

Robbins names an unglamorous practical cost of the D approach - it 'doesn't look as nice in the book,' which can trigger negative reactions from school leaders doing quality-assurance book checks, even when it is pedagogically stronger.

On feedback, Robbins favours cold-calling students whose answers he has tracked while circulating, over simple self-reported hands-up confidence checks, because it demonstrates to the class that the correct answer was attainable.
quotes: If we assume that "memory is the residue of thought" and "whoever does the thinking, does the learning" then some of these students clearly can make a stronger claim to have enhanced their learning than others.

B probably doesn't add anything to their learning. They are solely focused on writing neatly, as such the content of the sentence is probably broken down so much it loses its cohesion and the question is most likely not thought about.
C is interesting. They in theory have a score of 5/5 because they have thought about each question and retrieved the answer. However we have no evidence of this.
D seems like an easy case for a 5/5. Because they write the answer they are accountable and can prove they have thought about each question.
Yes it doesn't look as nice in the book, and this can require leaders to be educated on what a good book looks like because it will make their QA senses twitch.

I think many schools encourage A and B. Often the reason is given that "so students can look back in their books if they are stuck". For me I think this shows another misunderstanding of retrieval practice.
